newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada foreign minister blasts Nigeria "appeasers".
newsitem.headline: Canada foreign minister blasts Nigeria "appeasers".

text.p: Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy has bitterly attacked "appeasers" within the Commonwealth for trying to weaken sanctions against Nigeria's military regime.

Axworthy, stung by criticism of Canada's aggressive approach to sanctions, warned the Commonwealth in a newspaper interview published on Thursday that it risked allowing Nigeria to "get away with" executing author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other political dissidents last November.
"There are officials working on this in the Commonwealth who have lost all sight of what it's all about," Axworthy told the Toronto Globe and Mail in an interview from the United Nations.

"It's a sad commentary on the attitude of some people inside the Commonwealth that they're talking about flattering the Nigerians, who only a few months ago were executing political dissidents and are still engaged in the most active kind of repression," he said.

The Canadian foreign minister was reacting to a Reuters report from London on Wednesday in which some Commonwealth officials expressed irritation with Axworthy, saying he was needlessly antagonizing Nigeria.

"Axworthy seems to have lost the script on this one," said one unnamed Commonwealth official. "He does not understand that the Nigerians are a very proud people and you have to try to flatter them by making them feel important."

Axworthy hit back, saying the comment "sounds like a ploy by some of the appeasers inside the Commonwealth secretariat to try to soften even further the stand on Nigeria, which is already, I think, sadly diluted."
The Commonwealth's London-based secretariat has more than 300 employees and administers the affairs of the 53-nation Commonwealth, which groups Britain and its former colonies and protectorates.

Nigeria's military regime, led by Gen. Sani Abacha, in addition to executing the nine minority-rights activists, has jailed hundreds of other dissidents and repeatedly delayed its own target dates to hold national elections.

The country, which became independent in 1960, was suspended from the Commonwealth after the executions last year. Commonwealth ministers also agreed on a package of sanctions that included a ban on sports links and arms sales, but not on oil imports, which are Nigeria's main source of export earnings.
Axworthy said he feared a Commonwealth ministers meeting set for this Saturday in New York would produce little progress on sanctions.
"We'll have our discussion this weekend, but it seems to me they're simply setting up the scenario for another delay ...," he told the Globe and Mail. "Time is getting awfully short."
